extracted.intended_audience: students and practitioners of crystallography/mineralogy; scientifically literate readers seeking an introduction to crystal form and classification
extracted.subtask_description: An introductory textbook chapter describing the fundamental laws, geometric conventions, projection/drawing methods, and the classification of crystalline forms into systems and classes (with emphasis on the cubic/isometric system and its simple forms).

rubrics_metrics.name: Law of the Constancy of Angle
rubrics_metrics.description: According to the first law, the angles between corresponding faces of all crystals of the same chemical substance are always the same and are characteristic of the substance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Historical basis (Steno); measured with a goniometer; used as a diagnostic property of substances — angles are invariant for a given substance regardless of external crystal shape.

rubrics_metrics.name: Law of Symmetry
rubrics_metrics.description: Crystals may, or may not, be symmetrical with respect to a point, a line or axis, and a plane; these 'elements of symmetry' are spoken of as a centre of symmetry, an axis of symmetry, and a plane of symmetry respectively.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Defines centre of symmetry (parallel paired faces), axes of symmetry (tetrad/triad/dyad/hexad with rotation orders 4, 3, 2, 6 respectively) and planes of symmetry (cubic and dodecahedral examples). Examples and counts are given for the octahedron/cube (e.g. an octahedron has thirteen axes of symmetry and nine planes of symmetry). Notes that some classes lack certain symmetry elements (hemihedral/tetartohedral modifications).

rubrics_metrics.name: Law of Rational Intercepts or Indices (Millerian notation)
rubrics_metrics.description: Take three crystallographic axes OX, OY, OZ from three edges; a face intercepts them at ratios OA:OB:OC which are written inversely as indices h:k:l. The denominators h, k and l are always rational whole numbers (rarely exceeding 6, usually 0, 1, 2 or 3).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Indices (hkl) are inversely proportional to intercepts; {hkl} denotes all faces of that simple form. Millerian notation (indices) is recommended for simplicity and utility in calculation; choose crystallographic axes coincident with symmetry axes to obtain simpler indices. Knowing indices and axial parameters allows calculation of all interfacial angles.

rubrics_metrics.name: Zones and Weiss's zone-law
rubrics_metrics.description: All faces which intersect in parallel edges lie in the same zone. A zone-axis is a line through the centre parallel to those edges and a zone-plane is perpendicular to it. The direction of intersection (zone-axis) of two planes (hkl) and (h'k'l') is given by zone-indices [uvw] with u = kl' - lk', v = lh' - hl', w = hk' - kh'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Weiss's zone-law: any face (h2k2l2) lying in that zone must satisfy h2*u + k2*v + l2*w = 0. Indices of a face may be obtained by addition of indices of adjacent faces in the same zone (example: (311) obtained from other faces). Examples of zones and zone-axes are given for cubes and zircon.

rubrics_metrics.name: Projection and drawing conventions (stereographic and gnomonic projections; orthographic/clinographic drawings)
rubrics_metrics.description: Represent faces by the directions of their normals (poles) on a sphere and project these poles to a plane. Stereographic projection projects poles to the equatorial plane via lines to the pole of the sphere; gnomonic projection projects from the centre onto a tangent plane (zones appear as straight lines).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Stereographic projection: poles and zone-circles fix face positions and zonal relations; commonly used for angular calculations via spherical trigonometry. Gnomonic projection: zones are straight lines, useful for certain representations. Clinographic (oblique) and orthographic (perpendicular) projections preserve parallelism of edges and are preferred for crystal drawings; true perspective is avoided because it breaks parallel edge representation. Practical drawing steps (placing faces, rotating crystal, raising eye for clinographic view) are described.

rubrics_metrics.name: Crystallographic axes and crystal 'elements' (parameters and angles)
rubrics_metrics.description: Crystallographic axes OX, OY, OZ are taken as three edges formed by intersection of three faces; the parametral plane and the intercepts OA:OB:OC are the parameters (usually a:b:c). The angles between axes and the ratios of parameter lengths are the 'elements' of the crystal and are constant and characteristic for all crystals of the same substance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Axes are usually chosen related to crystal symmetry (often coincident with symmetry axes) to simplify indices and forms. The elements (angles and a:b:c) define the six systems (e.g., cubic: axes at right angles and equal length).

rubrics_metrics.name: Classification into six crystal systems and thirty-two classes
rubrics_metrics.description: According to the mutual inclinations of the crystallographic axes and the lengths intercepted on them by the parametral plane, all crystals fall into one or other of six groups or systems, in each of which there are several classes depending on the degree of symmetry.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The six systems (cubic, tetragonal, orthorhombic, monoclinic, anorthic, hexagonal) are defined by axis inclinations and parameter ratios; within systems, classes differ by available symmetry elements. Historical notes: Weiss, Mohs, and others developed the systems; Hessel proved 32 possible symmetry types.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cubic (Isometric) system: definition and interfacial-angle formula
rubrics_metrics.description: In the cubic system the three crystallographic axes are all at right angles to each other and are equal in length (parallel to the edges of the cube). In this system the angle between any two faces P(hkl) and Q(pqr) is given by COS PQ = (hp + kq + lr) / sqrt[(h^2 + k^2 + l^2)(p^2 + q^2 + r^2)].
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because of the cubic metric (a = b = c, axes orthogonal), angles between faces with the same indices are fixed and the same in all substances crystallizing in the cubic system. In other systems interfacial angles vary with the substance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Holosymmetric (Holohedral) class: full symmetry elements and representative simple forms
rubrics_metrics.description: Crystals of this class possess the full number of elements of symmetry for the cubic type: three cubic planes of symmetry, six dodecahedral planes, three tetrad axes, four triad axes, six dyad axes, and a centre of symmetry.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Seven kinds of simple forms occur (cube {100}, octahedron {111}, rhombic dodecahedron {110}, and four others); the chapter lists indices, typical interfacial angles, and mineral examples (e.g., salt/fluorspar/galena for cubes; spinel/gold for octahedra; garnet for rhombic dodecahedron). Notes which forms have fixed indices/angles and which vary.

rubrics_metrics.name: Simple forms and combinations; truncation
rubrics_metrics.description: A 'simple form' is a set of similar faces obtained by symmetrical repetition; a 'combination' is when two or more simple forms are present on one crystal. Truncation replaces edges or corners by new faces equally inclined to the faces forming the edge or corner.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: cube and octahedron as simple forms; cubo-octahedron and combinations shown in figures. Truncation operations (replace corners by faces) explain derivation of many combined forms; the resulting combination retains the symmetry elements of its constituent simple forms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Families of cubic simple forms with variable indices
rubrics_metrics.description: Several cubic simple forms form series in which face inclinations (and thus indices) vary: triakis-octahedron {hhk} (series {221},{331},{332}...), icositetrahedron {hkk} ({211},{311},{322}...), tetrakis-hexahedron {hko} ({210},{310},{320}...), and hexakis-octahedron {hkl} (general form {321},{421},{432}...).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These forms may approximate or combine with other cubic forms (e.g., tetrakis-hexahedron approximates cube or rhombic dodecahedron depending on inclinations). Some of these occur frequently in minerals (analcite, leucite, garnet, fluorspar) and the hexakis-octahedron is the greatest number of faces possible for a simple form (48). Their indices indicate which axes are intercepted and how faces vary across the series.

rubrics_metrics.name: Optical classification and its correspondence to crystal systems
rubrics_metrics.description: Crystals can be divided optically into isotropic, uniaxial and biaxial classes (Brewster). These optical classes correspond broadly to crystallographic systems: cubic crystals are isotropic, tetragonal and hexagonal are uniaxial, orthorhombic (and later monoclinic/anorthic distinctions) correspond to biaxial crystals.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Historical development (Brewster, Herschel, Neumann) and caveat: optical anomalies and exceptions exist; optical characters have been used to help establish and distinguish systems and classes.
